questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(1) · Term of the auditor
questions.stem: Under section 139(1) of the Companies Act 2013, an auditor appointed at the first annual general meeting holds office:

readLink.label: Read: Appointment at the first AGM — s. 139(1) →

options.text: For one year, from the conclusion of that meeting till the conclusion of the next annual general meeting
options.explanation: That is the tenure of an auditor of a GOVERNMENT company appointed by the C&AG under s. 139(5), and of an auditor appointed to fill a casual vacancy. It is not the s. 139(1) term.

options.text: For five years, from the date of the appointment till the fifth anniversary of that date
options.explanation: The term is not measured in calendar years from the date of appointment. Section 139(1) measures it in MEETINGS — from the conclusion of one to the conclusion of the sixth.

options.text: From the conclusion of that meeting till the conclusion of its sixth annual general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(1) fixes the term from the conclusion of the meeting of appointment till the conclusion of the sixth annual general meeting, and thereafter till the conclusion of every sixth meeting. Five sets of annual accounts are audited.

options.text: From the conclusion of that meeting till the conclusion of its fifth annual general meeting, subject to ratification at each intervening meeting
options.explanation: Two errors. The term runs to the SIXTH meeting, not the fifth; and the ratification proviso was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2017.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(1) · Consent and eligibility certificate
questions.stem: Before appointing an auditor under section 139(1), a company must obtain from the proposed auditor:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 139(1) and first proviso

readLink.label: Read: Appointment at the first AGM — s. 139(1) →

options.text: His written consent, and a certificate that the appointment, if made, will be in accordance with the prescribed conditions, indicating whether he satisfies the criteria in section 141
options.explanation: Correct. Both documents are pre-conditions of the appointment: written consent, and a certificate that also addresses the s. 141 eligibility and disqualification criteria.

options.text: Only his written consent; the certificate is required only where the company is listed
options.explanation: The certificate is required for every company, not only a listed one. Listing matters for rotation under s. 139(2), not for the consent-and-certificate requirement.

options.text: Only a certificate of practice issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India
options.explanation: A certificate of practice evidences that he may practise; it says nothing about the specific appointment or the s. 141 criteria, which is what the proviso requires.

options.text: A no-objection certificate from the retiring auditor and his written consent
options.explanation: The Companies Act imposes no statutory no-objection requirement on the incoming auditor. Professional communication with the retiring auditor is a Chartered Accountants Act matter, not a s. 139 condition.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(1) · Ratification omitted
questions.stem: Which statement about ratification of an auditor's appointment is correct for the law as on 28 February 2026?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 139(1) — proviso omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2017

readLink.label: Read: Appointment at the first AGM — s. 139(1) →

options.text: The appointment must be ratified by the members by ordinary resolution at every annual general meeting during the term
options.explanation: This was the position under the omitted proviso to s. 139(1). It is a pre-2018 answer and is no longer the law.

options.text: The appointment must be ratified by the Board at every annual general meeting during the term
options.explanation: Ratification was never a Board function even when the proviso stood; it was for the members. And the requirement no longer exists at all.

options.text: Ratification is required only for listed companies and companies covered by the rotation rules
options.explanation: There is no such split. The requirement was omitted for every class of company alike.

options.text: No ratification is required; the requirement was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2017 and the auditor holds office for the whole term
options.explanation: Correct. Since the omission the auditor holds office for the full five-meeting term unless he resigns, is removed under s. 140, or vacates office under s. 141(4).

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(10) · No appointment at the AGM
questions.stem: Where at any annual general meeting no auditor is appointed or re-appointed, section 139(10) provides that:

readLink.label: Read: Appointment at the first AGM — s. 139(1) →

options.text: A casual vacancy arises which the Board must fill within thirty days
options.explanation: No vacancy arises. A casual vacancy is a vacancy arising otherwise than by efflux of time; here the section itself keeps the office filled.

options.text: The existing auditor shall continue to be the auditor of the company
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(10) keeps the existing auditor in office so that the company is never left without an auditor merely because the members failed to act.

options.text: The Central Government shall appoint an auditor on the company's application
options.explanation: That was the position under the earlier legislation. Section 139(10) of the 2013 Act solves the problem internally, without any Central Government appointment.

options.text: The Registrar shall appoint an auditor for the remainder of the financial year
options.explanation: The Registrar has no power of appointment under Chapter X. The only external appointing authorities are the C&AG (s. 139(5) and (7)) and the Central Government after a Tribunal order under s. 140(5).

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(1) · Notice to the Registrar (ADT-1)
questions.stem: Sindhutai Foods Limited appoints M/s Kalyani & Associates as its auditors at its annual general meeting held on 25 August 2026. The audit committee had recommended the firm on 30 July 2026 and the engagement letter was signed on 2 September 2026. The last date for the company to file notice of the appointment with the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 139(1) — notice within fifteen days of the meeting

readLink.label: Read: Appointment at the first AGM — s. 139(1) →

options.text: 24 September 2026
options.explanation: This counts thirty days from the meeting. The s. 139(1) period is fifteen days; thirty days is the s. 139(6) and s. 139(8) appointment window, not the filing window.

options.text: 9 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Fifteen days from the date of the MEETING (25 August 2026) expires on 9 September 2026. The audit committee's recommendation and the engagement letter are irrelevant to this clock.

options.text: 8 September 2026
options.explanation: An off-by-one: this counts fourteen days. Day one is the day after the meeting, so the fifteenth day is 9 September.

options.text: 25 September 2026
options.explanation: This reads the period as one calendar month. Section 139(1) says fifteen days, and days are counted as days.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(6) · First auditor, non-government company
questions.stem: Chandravali Foods Limited, which is not a government company, is registered on 12 May 2026. The last date by which its Board of Directors must appoint the first auditor is:

readLink.label: Read: The first auditor and casual vacancies →

options.text: 11 June 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(6) gives the Board thirty days from the date of registration; 12 May 2026 plus thirty days is 11 June 2026.

options.text: 10 August 2026
options.explanation: This counts ninety days. Ninety days is the members' window at an extraordinary general meeting AFTER the Board has failed, not the Board's own window.

options.text: 11 July 2026
options.explanation: This counts sixty days, which is the C&AG's window for a GOVERNMENT company under s. 139(7). The company here is not a government company.

options.text: 12 August 2026
options.explanation: This reads the period as three calendar months. Section 139(6) states thirty days.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(6) · Tenure of the first auditor
questions.stem: A first auditor appointed by the Board of a non-government company under section 139(6) holds office:

readLink.label: Read: The first auditor and casual vacancies →

options.text: Till the conclusion of the sixth annual general meeting
options.explanation: That is the term of an auditor appointed at the first annual general meeting under s. 139(1). A first auditor appointed by the Board does not get a five-meeting term.

options.text: For one year from the date of his appointment by the Board
options.explanation: The tenure is not measured from the date of appointment; it ends at a meeting, whenever that meeting is held.

options.text: Till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(6) ends the first auditor's office at the conclusion of the first annual general meeting, at which the members then make the s. 139(1) appointment.

options.text: Till the members remove him by special resolution with the previous approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: That describes removal under s. 140(1), which is a way an auditor may leave office early. It is not the natural tenure fixed by s. 139(6).

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(7) · First auditor, government company
questions.stem: Sarayu Power Limited, a government company, is registered on 3 August 2026. The last date by which the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India must appoint its first auditor is:

readLink.label: Read: The first auditor and casual vacancies →

options.text: 2 September 2026
options.explanation: This counts thirty days, which is the Board's window for a non-government company under s. 139(6) and the Board's fallback window under s. 139(7).

options.text: 1 November 2026
options.explanation: This counts ninety days. Ninety days appears in s. 139(6) as the members' window for a non-government company, not in s. 139(7).

options.text: 2 October 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(7) gives the C&AG sixty days from the date of registration; 3 August 2026 plus sixty days is 2 October 2026.

options.text: 30 January 2027
options.explanation: This counts 180 days, which is the s. 139(5) period for appointing a SUBSEQUENT auditor of a government company and runs from the commencement of the financial year, not from registration.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(7) · Failure of the C&AG to appoint
questions.stem: Where the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India does not appoint the first auditor of a government company within the period allowed by section 139(7), the appointment is then to be made by:

readLink.label: Read: The first auditor and casual vacancies →

options.text: The members at an extraordinary general meeting within thirty days
options.explanation: The members are the third step, not the second, and their window is sixty days, not thirty.

options.text: The Central Government, on an application by the company
options.explanation: The Central Government appoints an auditor only after a Tribunal order under s. 140(5). It has no role in the s. 139(7) chain.

options.text: The Registrar, within thirty days of being informed by the company
options.explanation: The Registrar has no power of appointment under Chapter X; his role is to receive the notice of appointment.

options.text: The Board of Directors, within the next thirty days; and on the Board's failure, by the members at an extraordinary general meeting within sixty days
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(7) runs 60 days (C&AG) → 30 days (Board) → 60 days (members at an EGM), the auditor in every case holding office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(5) · Subsequent auditor of a government company
questions.stem: For a government company whose financial year commences on 1 April 2026, the last date by which the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India must appoint the auditor for that year is:

readLink.label: Read: The first auditor and casual vacancies →

options.explanation: This counts sixty days, which is the s. 139(7) window for appointing the FIRST auditor of a government company and runs from registration.

options.text: 30 June 2026
options.explanation: This counts ninety days, a period that belongs to s. 139(6) and to a non-government company.

options.text: 1 October 2026
options.explanation: This reads 180 days as six calendar months. The section says one hundred and eighty days, and days are counted as days.

options.text: 28 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(5) allows 180 days from the commencement of the financial year; 1 April 2026 plus 180 days is 28 September 2026. That auditor holds office till the conclusion of the annual general meeting.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(8) · What is a casual vacancy
questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT create a casual vacancy in the office of auditor?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, ss. 139(8), 140(5) Explanation I and 141(4)

readLink.label: Read: The first auditor and casual vacancies →

options.text: The expiry of the auditor's term at the conclusion of the sixth annual general meeting
options.explanation: Correct as the exception. A vacancy arising by efflux of time is not casual; the office is filled by an ordinary appointment under s. 139(1), not under s. 139(8).

options.text: The death of the auditor during his term
options.explanation: This is the paradigm casual vacancy — a vacancy arising otherwise than by efflux of time — and is filled by the Board within thirty days.

options.text: The auditor incurring a disqualification under section 141(3) after his appointment
options.explanation: Section 141(4) makes him vacate office and expressly deems that vacation to be a casual vacancy.

options.text: An order of the Tribunal under section 140(5) directing the company to change its auditor
options.explanation: Explanation I to s. 140(5) deems the vacancy so created to be a casual vacancy in the office of the auditor.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(8)(i) · Casual vacancy by resignation
questions.stem: The auditor of Rukmini Textiles Limited, which is not a government company, resigns on 2 July 2026. The Board recommends a replacement on 10 July 2026 and appoints him on 20 July 2026. The last date by which the members must approve that appointment in general meeting is:

readLink.label: Read: The first auditor and casual vacancies →

options.text: 9 August 2026
options.explanation: This counts thirty days from the Board's recommendation. Thirty days is the Board's window to FILL the vacancy; the members' approval has a separate three-month window.

options.text: 10 October 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Where the casual vacancy results from a resignation, the appointment must also be approved by the company at a general meeting convened within three months of the Board's RECOMMENDATION — 10 July 2026 plus three months is 10 October 2026.

options.text: 8 October 2026
options.explanation: This counts ninety days rather than three calendar months. Section 139(8)(i) expresses the period in months, which land on the same day of the later month.

options.text: 10 January 2027
options.explanation: This counts six months. The section allows three.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(8)(ii) · Casual vacancy in a C&AG company
questions.stem: A casual vacancy arises in the office of the auditor of a company whose accounts are subject to audit by an auditor appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India. The vacancy is to be filled:

readLink.label: Read: The first auditor and casual vacancies →

options.text: By the Board within thirty days, and where the vacancy arose by resignation, with the members' approval within three months
options.explanation: That is s. 139(8)(i), which applies to companies OTHER than those audited by a C&AG-appointed auditor.

options.text: By the members at an extraordinary general meeting within ninety days
options.explanation: Ninety days is the members' window under s. 139(6) for a first auditor of a non-government company. It has no place in s. 139(8)(ii).

options.text: By the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India within thirty days; and if he does not fill it, by the Board within the next thirty days
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(8)(ii) gives the C&AG thirty days and, on his failure, gives the Board a further thirty days.

options.text: By the Central Government within thirty days of being informed by the Board
options.explanation: The Central Government appoints an auditor only under s. 140(5) after a Tribunal order. It plays no part in filling a casual vacancy.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(2) · Rotation tenure
questions.stem: In a company to which section 139(2) applies, the maximum tenure permitted is:

readLink.label: Read: Rotation of auditors →

options.text: One term of five consecutive years for an individual, and two terms of five consecutive years for an audit firm
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(2)(a) caps an individual at one term of five consecutive years; s. 139(2)(b) caps an audit firm at two such terms, that is ten years.

options.text: Two terms of five consecutive years for an individual, and one term of five consecutive years for an audit firm
options.explanation: The two limbs are reversed. The firm gets the longer tenure, not the individual.

options.text: One term of five consecutive years for both an individual and an audit firm
options.explanation: This ignores s. 139(2)(b), which expressly gives an audit firm two terms.

options.text: Two terms of five consecutive years for both an individual and an audit firm
options.explanation: This ignores s. 139(2)(a). An individual gets one term only.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(2) · Companies covered by rotation
questions.stem: Apart from listed companies, the rotation requirement in section 139(2) currently applies to the prescribed classes, which include:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 139(2) read with Rule 5, Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014 (rules-level, amendment-sensitive)

readLink.label: Read: Rotation of auditors →

options.text: All unlisted public companies and all private companies, without any capital threshold
options.explanation: The rule is threshold-based. A blanket application to every unlisted public and private company would sweep in small companies and one-person companies, which the rule leaves out.

options.text: Unlisted public companies having paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore or more, private companies having paid-up share capital of ₹50 crore or more, and companies having public borrowings from financial institutions, banks or public deposits of ₹50 crore or more
options.explanation: Correct as the position stated in these notes. Note that all three figures sit in the Rules, not in the section, and are amendment-sensitive.

options.text: Only companies in which the Central or a State Government holds not less than 51% of the paid-up share capital
options.explanation: That is the test of a government company under s. 2(45), which governs who APPOINTS the auditor under s. 139(5) and (7). It has nothing to do with rotation.

options.text: Only companies required to constitute an audit committee under section 177
options.explanation: The audit committee classes and the rotation classes overlap but are prescribed separately and are not the same set. Section 139(2) does not use the audit committee as its trigger.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(2) · Cooling-off after two terms
questions.stem: Nairit Alloys Limited is a listed company. M/s Deshmukh & Co, an audit firm, was appointed at the annual general meeting held in 2016 for a term of five years and re-appointed at the meeting held in 2021 for a second term of five years, its tenure ending at the conclusion of the meeting held in 2026. The earliest annual general meeting at which the firm may again be appointed as auditor of that company is the one held in:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 139(2)(b) and the second proviso

readLink.label: Read: Rotation of auditors →

options.explanation: This applies a three-year cooling-off. The proviso to s. 139(2) prescribes five years, not three; three years was the transition window for existing companies to comply, an entirely different provision.

Correct. The firm completes its two terms at the conclusion of the 2026 meeting and is ineligible for re-appointment in that company for five years from the completion of the terms, so the 2031 meeting is the earliest.
This adds ten years, confusing the firm's ten-year TENURE with the five-year cooling-off. The cooling-off is five years for an individual and a firm alike.
This treats the bar as lasting one year. Section 139(2) bars re-appointment for five years from the completion of the term.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(2) · Common partner and network
questions.stem: An audit firm's tenure in a listed company expired at the end of the immediately preceding financial year. Which of the following firms may nevertheless be appointed as the company's auditor?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 139(2), third proviso, read with the network and retiring-partner rules

readLink.label: Read: Rotation of auditors →

options.text: A firm having one partner in common with the outgoing firm
options.explanation: Barred. No audit firm having a common partner or partners with the outgoing firm whose tenure has expired may be appointed for five years; one common partner is enough.

options.text: A firm belonging to the same network as the outgoing firm, operating under a common brand name
options.explanation: Barred. The network rule reaches firms operating or marketed under a common brand name or under common control, which is exactly the avoidance the rule is aimed at.

options.text: A firm which the partner in charge of the outgoing audit, who certified the financial statements, has joined after retiring from the outgoing firm
options.explanation: Barred. Where such a partner moves, the firm he joins is itself ineligible for five years.

options.text: A firm having no common partner with the outgoing firm, not belonging to its network, and not joined by the partner who was in charge of the outgoing audit
options.explanation: Correct. Once the common-partner bar, the network bar and the retiring-partner bar are all cleared, nothing in s. 139(2) prevents the appointment.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(3) · Members may go further
questions.stem: Section 139(3) permits a resolution to be passed providing that the auditing partner and his team shall be rotated at specified intervals, or that the audit shall be conducted by more than one auditor. That resolution is passed by:

readLink.label: Read: Rotation of auditors →

options.text: The members of the company
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(3) is a members' power, letting them tighten rotation beyond what the Act requires. They can never loosen s. 139(2).

options.text: The Board of Directors
options.explanation: The Board has no such power. It appoints only the first auditor and fills casual vacancies; the internal rotation choice belongs to the members.

options.text: The audit committee constituted under section 177
options.explanation: The audit committee recommends the appointment where one is required, but s. 139(3) speaks of a resolution of the company, that is of the members.

options.text: The Central Government, by order under section 139(4)
options.explanation: Section 139(4) does empower the Central Government to prescribe the MANNER of rotation, but the s. 139(3) choice about partner rotation and joint auditors is the members'.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 140(1) · Special resolution for removal
questions.stem: The Board of Suvarna Ceramics Limited resolves on 18 May 2026 to remove its auditor before the expiry of his term. The Central Government's approval is received on 8 June 2026. The last date by which the company must pass the special resolution is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 140(1) read with Rule 7, Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Removal, resignation and the special-notice route →

options.text: 8 July 2026
options.explanation: This counts thirty days. Thirty days is the window for the APPLICATION to the Central Government, counted from the Board resolution; the resolution window is longer and starts later.

options.text: 8 August 2026
options.explanation: This reads the period as two calendar months. The requirement is sixty days, and days are counted as days.

options.text: 7 August 2026
options.explanation: Correct. The general meeting for the special resolution must be held within sixty days of RECEIPT of the Central Government's approval; 8 June 2026 plus sixty days is 7 August 2026.

options.text: 6 September 2026
options.explanation: This counts ninety days, a period that does not appear anywhere in s. 140.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 140(1) · Application to the Central Government
questions.stem: The application to the Central Government for its previous approval to the removal of an auditor before the expiry of his term must be made:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 140(1) read with Rule 7, Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Removal, resignation and the special-notice route →

options.text: Within thirty days of the passing of the special resolution
options.explanation: This inverts the sequence. The approval is a PREVIOUS approval: it must be obtained before the special resolution, not after it.

options.text: Within thirty days of the resolution of the Board
options.explanation: Correct. The application in the prescribed form goes to the Central Government within thirty days of the Board resolution; the special resolution then follows within sixty days of receiving the approval.

options.text: Within sixty days of the resolution of the Board
options.explanation: Sixty days is the period for holding the general meeting after the approval is received. The application window is thirty days.

options.text: Within fifteen days of the general meeting at which the auditor was removed
options.explanation: Fifteen days is the s. 139(1) window for notifying the Registrar of an APPOINTMENT. It has nothing to do with removal.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 140(2) · Resignation statement (ADT-3)
questions.stem: The auditor of Kaustubh Chemicals Limited, which is not a government company, resigns on 18 September 2026. The last date by which he must file the prescribed statement of resignation with the company and the Registrar is:

readLink.label: Read: Removal, resignation and the special-notice route →

options.text: 3 October 2026
options.explanation: This counts fifteen days. Fifteen days is the s. 139(1) period for the company's notice of an appointment to the Registrar.

options.text: 2 November 2026
options.explanation: This counts forty-five days, which is the period allowed to the Board or audit committee to reply to a fraud report under the s. 143(12) machinery.

options.text: 25 September 2026
options.explanation: This counts seven days, a period that does not appear in s. 140.

options.text: 18 October 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 140(2) requires the statement within thirty days from the date of resignation; 18 September 2026 plus thirty days is 18 October 2026. The duty is the auditor's own, and in a government company the statement also goes to the C&AG.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 140(5) · Consequences of a fraud finding
questions.stem: Where the Tribunal passes a final order under section 140(5) against an auditor who has acted in a fraudulent manner, the auditor:

readLink.label: Read: Removal, resignation and the special-notice route →

options.text: Is not eligible to be appointed as an auditor of any company for five years from the date of the order, and is also liable for action under section 447
options.explanation: Correct. The debarment under the second proviso to s. 140(5) is across ALL companies, and s. 447 liability for fraud follows independently.

options.text: Is not eligible to be appointed as an auditor of that company for five years, but may audit other companies
options.explanation: This confuses the s. 140(5) debarment with the s. 139(2) rotation cooling-off, which alone is company-specific.

options.text: Is not eligible to be appointed as an auditor of any company for ten years
options.explanation: Ten years is the s. 141(3)(h) period following a conviction for an offence involving fraud. The s. 140(5) debarment is five years.

options.text: Is permanently debarred from acting as an auditor of any company
options.explanation: The Act prescribes a five-year debarment, not a permanent one. Permanent consequences, if any, would follow from disciplinary action under the Chartered Accountants Act.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 140(4) · Special notice and its exception
questions.stem: Special notice under section 140(4) is required for a resolution at an annual general meeting appointing a person other than the retiring auditor, EXCEPT where:

readLink.label: Read: Removal, resignation and the special-notice route →

options.text: The retiring auditor has given the company a notice in writing of his unwillingness to be re-appointed
options.explanation: Unwillingness is a ground on which s. 139(9) denies automatic re-appointment. It is not the exception the proviso to s. 140(4) states.

options.text: The retiring auditor has been removed earlier under section 140(1) with the approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: An auditor removed under s. 140(1) is no longer the retiring auditor at all, so the question of special notice does not arise in that form.

options.text: The retiring auditor has completed his consecutive tenure of five years, or ten years, as the case may be, under section 139(2)
options.explanation: Correct. Where rotation itself ends the auditor's office, no member need move anything and no special notice is required.

options.text: The company is not required to constitute an audit committee under section 177
options.explanation: The audit committee affects who recommends an appointment; it has no bearing on whether special notice is needed.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · ss. 141(1) and 141(2) · Firms and LLPs
questions.stem: Which statement about the appointment of a firm as auditor is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications →

options.text: A firm may be appointed by its firm name only if all its partners practising in India are chartered accountants
options.explanation: The test is a MAJORITY of the partners practising in India, not all of them.

options.text: A limited liability partnership cannot be appointed as auditor, being a body corporate
options.explanation: An LLP is the express exception to the body-corporate bar in s. 141(3)(a). It may be appointed.

options.text: Where a firm is appointed, any partner may act and sign on its behalf
options.explanation: Section 141(2) confines acting and signing to the partners who are chartered accountants. A non-chartered-accountant partner may neither act nor sign.

options.text: A firm, including a limited liability partnership, may be appointed by its firm name where a majority of its partners practising in India are chartered accountants, but only its chartered accountant partners may act and sign on its behalf
options.explanation: Correct. Three rules in one: majority of practising partners qualified (s. 141(1) proviso), an LLP is permitted (s. 141(3)(a) exception), and only chartered accountant partners act and sign (s. 141(2)).

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 141(3)(a) · Body corporate
questions.stem: Under section 141(3)(a), which of the following is NOT disqualified from being appointed as auditor of a company?

readLink.label: Read: Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications →

options.text: A private limited company whose directors are all chartered accountants
options.explanation: It is a body corporate and therefore disqualified, whatever the qualifications of its directors. The exception is confined to limited liability partnerships.

options.text: A limited liability partnership registered under the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008
options.explanation: Correct. An LLP is a body corporate but is the express exception in s. 141(3)(a) and may be appointed, subject to ss. 141(1) and 141(2).

options.text: A public company incorporated to provide audit and assurance services
options.explanation: A body corporate, and so disqualified. The object for which it was incorporated makes no difference.

options.text: A foreign company registered in India carrying on an accountancy practice
options.explanation: A foreign company is a body corporate and is not a limited liability partnership registered under the 2008 Act, so the exception does not reach it.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 141(3)(d)(i) · Relative holding securities
questions.stem: Regarding the holding of securities in a company by the auditor and his relatives, which statement is correct?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 141(3)(d)(i) and its provisos, read with Rule 10 (rules-level)

readLink.label: Read: Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications →

options.text: A relative may hold securities of face value not exceeding ₹1,00,000, and where a relative acquires securities beyond that limit the auditor may take corrective action within sixty days
options.explanation: Correct. The relief is for a relative alone, capped by FACE value, with a sixty-day corrective window when the limit is crossed by a later acquisition.

options.text: The auditor himself may hold securities of face value not exceeding ₹1,00,000
options.explanation: The relief runs only to a relative. The auditor and his partner may hold no security or interest at all in the company, its subsidiary, its holding or associate company, or a subsidiary of that holding company.

options.text: The limit of ₹1,00,000 is measured by the market value of the securities on the date of appointment
options.explanation: The limit is expressed in FACE value, which does not move with the market. Using market value is the standard misreading.

options.text: The bar applies only to securities of the company itself and not to those of its holding, subsidiary or associate companies
options.explanation: The clause expressly extends to the company, its subsidiary, its holding company, its associate company and a subsidiary of such holding company.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 147(2) · The two limbs of the auditor's punishment
questions.stem: An auditor contravenes section 143 knowingly and wilfully, with the intention of deceiving the company's shareholders. Under section 147(2) he is liable to:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 147(2) and its proviso (amounts amendment-sensitive)

readLink.label: Read: Punishment for contravention — s. 147 →

options.text: A fine only, capped at the lower of ₹5,00,000 and four times his remuneration
options.explanation: That is the FIRST limb, which applies to an ordinary contravention. Once the contravention is knowing or wilful with intent to deceive, the proviso takes over.

options.text: Imprisonment only, for a term which may extend to one year
options.explanation: The proviso imposes imprisonment AND a fine, not imprisonment alone.

options.text: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year and a fine capped at the lower of ₹25,00,000 and eight times his remuneration
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 147(2) applies where the contravention is knowing or wilful with intent to deceive the company, its shareholders, creditors or the tax authorities: imprisonment up to one year together with a fine measured against ₹25,00,000 or eight times the remuneration, whichever is less.

options.text: A fine capped at the lower of ₹25,00,000 and eight times his remuneration, but no imprisonment, imprisonment having been removed by amendment
options.explanation: Imprisonment was removed for OFFICERS in default under s. 147(1). It survives in the wilful limb of s. 147(2) for the auditor.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 141(3)(g) · Counting the twenty
questions.stem: CA Rajan currently holds appointment as auditor of 9 unlisted public companies, 4 listed companies, 3 one-person companies, 2 dormant companies, 5 small companies and 6 private companies, of which one has a paid-up share capital of ₹140 crore and the remaining five have paid-up share capital below ₹100 crore. Applying the exclusions prescribed for section 141(3)(g), the number of further company audits he may accept is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 141(3)(g) read with the prescribed exclusions (rules-level, amendment-sensitive)

readLink.label: Read: Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications →

options.text: Nil — he already holds more than twenty audits
options.explanation: This counts all 29 appointments. One-person companies, dormant companies, small companies and private companies with paid-up capital below ₹100 crore are excluded from the reckoning.
This excludes the one-person, dormant and small companies but counts all six private companies. Five of them, being below ₹100 crore of paid-up capital, are also excluded.
Correct. Counted: 9 unlisted public + 4 listed + 1 private company of ₹140 crore = 14. The ceiling being twenty, he may accept 6 more.
This counts only the 9 unlisted public companies and forgets that listed companies and large private companies count too.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 141(3)(g) · Exclusions from the ceiling
questions.stem: In reckoning the limit of twenty companies under section 141(3)(g), which of the following is NOT excluded?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 141(3)(g) read with the prescribed exclusions (rules-level, amendment-sensitive)

readLink.label: Read: Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications →

options.text: One person companies
options.explanation: Expressly excluded from the reckoning.

options.text: Dormant companies
options.explanation: Expressly excluded from the reckoning.

options.text: Private companies having paid-up share capital of less than ₹100 crore
options.explanation: Expressly excluded. Note the direction of the test: it is the SMALLER private companies that fall out of the count.

options.text: Unlisted public companies having paid-up share capital of less than ₹100 crore
options.explanation: Correct as the exception. The paid-up capital carve-out is confined to PRIVATE companies. Every public company, listed or unlisted and whatever its capital, counts towards the twenty.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 141(3)(d)(i) · Curing a relative's holding
questions.stem: The brother of CA Meghna holds 1,200 equity shares of face value ₹100 each in Tarangini Structures Limited, which proposes to appoint her as its auditor. The minimum number of those shares that must cease to be held by him for the relative's holding to be within the prescribed limit is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 141(3)(d)(i), first proviso, read with Rule 10 (rules-level: ₹1,00,000 face value)

readLink.label: Read: Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications →

options.text: 200 shares
options.explanation: Correct. The holding is 1,200 × ₹100 = ₹1,20,000 of face value against a permitted ₹1,00,000, an excess of ₹20,000, which is 200 shares of ₹100 each. Corrective action must in any event be taken within sixty days where the limit is crossed by an acquisition.

options.text: 1,200 shares — the entire holding
options.explanation: This applies the auditor's own position to a relative. A relative is permitted to hold up to ₹1,00,000 of face value; only the excess must go.

options.text: 20 shares
options.explanation: This treats the ₹20,000 excess as if the shares had a face value of ₹1,000 each. They have a face value of ₹100 each, so 200 shares are needed.

options.text: 1,000 shares
options.explanation: This subtracts the permitted number of shares from the total in the wrong direction — it would leave the relative with 200 shares when he may hold 1,000.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · ss. 145 and 146 · Signing, reading and attendance
questions.stem: Which statement about sections 145 and 146 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Signing, reading and attendance →

options.text: The whole of the auditor's report must be read out before the company in general meeting
options.explanation: Only the qualifications, observations or comments on financial transactions or matters having an adverse effect on the functioning of the company must be read out.

options.text: The auditor shall, unless otherwise exempted by the company, attend every general meeting either himself or through an authorised representative who is qualified to be an auditor, and has the right to be heard on business which concerns him as auditor
options.explanation: Correct. Attendance is a duty subject only to an exemption given by the company, the representative must himself be qualified to be an auditor, and the right to be heard is limited to business concerning him as auditor.

options.text: Attendance at general meetings is purely a right of the auditor, which he may exercise or not as he chooses
options.explanation: Section 146 uses the word 'shall'. It is a duty as well as a right, displaced only by an exemption from the company.

options.text: Any partner of the audit firm may sign the auditor's report on behalf of the firm
options.explanation: Section 145 requires signature in accordance with s. 141(2), which confines acting and signing to the partners who are chartered accountants.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 142 · Remuneration
questions.stem: Which statement about the remuneration of an auditor under section 142 is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Remuneration of auditors — s. 142 →

options.text: It is fixed in general meeting or in such manner as may be determined therein, except that the Board may fix the remuneration of the first auditor
options.explanation: Correct. Section 142(1) puts remuneration with the members, and its proviso carves out the first auditor, whose remuneration the Board may fix.

options.text: It is fixed by the Board in every case, subject to ratification by the members
options.explanation: This inverts the rule and the exception. The members fix it; only the first auditor's remuneration may be fixed by the Board.

options.text: It includes the fee payable and any sum paid to the auditor for other services rendered at the company's request
options.explanation: Section 142(2) expressly EXCLUDES remuneration for other services. This matters because s. 147(2) measures the auditor's fine as a multiple of his remuneration.

options.text: It excludes expenses incurred by the auditor in connection with the audit and facilities extended to him
options.explanation: Those are expressly INCLUDED by s. 142(2), along with the fee payable.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 143(1) · The six inquiry matters
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the matters the auditor is required to inquire into under section 143(1)?

readLink.label: Read: Powers and duties of auditors — s. 143 →

options.text: Whether loans and advances made by the company on the basis of security have been properly secured and whether the terms on which they have been made are prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members
options.explanation: This is clause (a) of s. 143(1).

options.text: Whether personal expenses have been charged to revenue account
options.explanation: This is clause (e) of s. 143(1).

options.text: Where shares are stated in the books to have been allotted for cash, whether cash has actually been received and, if not, whether the position stated in the books and the balance sheet is correct, regular and not misleading
options.explanation: This is clause (f) of s. 143(1).

options.text: Whether the company has complied with the provisions relating to the acceptance of deposits from the public
options.explanation: Correct as the exception. Deposit compliance is a reporting matter that may arise under the order made under s. 143(11), not one of the six inquiry matters listed in s. 143(1).

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 143(1) and 143(3) · Access and report contents
questions.stem: Which statement about the auditor's right of access and the contents of his report is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Powers and duties of auditors — s. 143 →

options.text: The auditor's right of access is confined to the books and vouchers kept at the registered office
options.explanation: Section 143(1) gives access to the books and vouchers whether kept at the registered office or at any other place.

options.text: The auditor of a holding company has no right of access to the records of its subsidiaries
options.explanation: The proviso to s. 143(1) gives the holding company's auditor access to the records of all subsidiaries and associate companies so far as it relates to the consolidation of financial statements.

options.text: The report must state whether any director is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2), and whether the company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements and their operating effectiveness
options.explanation: Correct. These are clauses (g) and (i) of s. 143(3); the internal financial controls clause is subject to a rules-level exemption for certain private companies.

options.text: Where a matter required to be stated in the report is answered in the negative, the auditor need not state his reasons
options.explanation: Section 143(4) requires the report to state the reasons wherever a matter is answered in the negative or with a qualification.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · ss. 143(6) and 143(8) · C&AG and branch audit
questions.stem: Which statement about sections 143(6) and 143(8) is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Powers and duties of auditors — s. 143 →

options.text: The C&AG may, within sixty days of receiving the audit report, conduct a supplementary audit and comment upon or supplement the report, the comments being sent to the company and placed before the annual general meeting in the same manner as the audit report
options.explanation: Correct. That is the whole of s. 143(6), including the requirement that the comments travel to the members alongside the audit report.

options.text: The C&AG may conduct a supplementary audit at any time within three years of receiving the audit report
options.explanation: The period is sixty days from the date of receipt of the audit report.

options.text: The accounts of a branch office must in every case be audited by the company's own auditor
options.explanation: Section 143(8) also permits another person qualified for appointment as auditor and appointed under s. 139, and for a foreign branch a person qualified under the law of that country.

options.text: The branch auditor sends his report directly to the members of the company
options.explanation: The branch auditor sends his report to the COMPANY'S auditor, who deals with it in his own report as he considers necessary.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 143(12) · The first step on discovering fraud
questions.stem: An auditor has reason to believe that officers of the company have committed a fraud involving ₹4 crore. His first step is to:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 143(12) read with Rule 13, Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Reporting of fraud →

options.text: Report the matter directly to the Central Government within two days, the amount exceeding ₹1 crore
options.explanation: Even above ₹1 crore the Central Government is never the first recipient. The auditor must first go to the Board or the audit committee.

options.text: Report the matter to the Board or the audit committee immediately and not later than two days of his knowledge, seeking their reply or observations within forty-five days
options.explanation: Correct. The first step is always internal and always within two days; the Central Government is reached only after the forty-five-day reply window.

options.text: Qualify his audit report and take no further step, the matter being covered by section 143(3)(f)
options.explanation: Qualification does not discharge the s. 143(12) duty, which is a separate and mandatory reporting obligation.

options.text: Report the matter to the Registrar within thirty days and disclose it in the Board's report
options.explanation: The Registrar is not a recipient under s. 143(12), and the Board's-report disclosure is the route for frauds BELOW the prescribed amount, not for this one.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 144 · Prohibited services
questions.stem: Which of the following services is NOT included in the list of services an auditor is prohibited from rendering under section 144?

readLink.label: Read: Services an auditor must not render — s. 144 →

options.text: Design and implementation of any financial information system
options.explanation: Expressly prohibited by s. 144.

options.text: Actuarial services
options.explanation: Expressly prohibited by s. 144.

options.text: Taxation services, such as representing the company before the tax authorities
options.explanation: Correct as the exception. Taxation services are not in the s. 144 list; they may be rendered, but only with the approval of the Board or the audit committee as s. 144 itself requires for any other service.

options.text: Rendering of outsourced financial services
options.explanation: Expressly prohibited by s. 144, and the prohibition bites whether the service is rendered directly or indirectly.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 148(6) · Filing the cost audit report
questions.stem: Prathama Cements Limited receives a copy of its cost audit report from the cost auditor on 12 August 2026. The last date by which the company must furnish the report to the Central Government, with full information and explanation on every reservation or qualification in it, is:

readLink.label: Read: Cost records and cost audit — s. 148 →

options.text: 27 August 2026
options.explanation: This counts fifteen days. Section 148(6) allows thirty days from the date of receipt of the report.

options.text: 11 October 2026
options.explanation: This counts sixty days, a period that does not appear in s. 148.

options.text: 12 September 2026
options.explanation: This reads the period as one calendar month. The section says thirty days, and days are counted as days.

options.text: 11 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days from 12 August 2026 expires on 11 September 2026. The clock runs from the company's RECEIPT of the report, not from the end of the financial year.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · ss. 139(6), 139(7) and 139(8) · First auditor and casual vacancy
questions.stem: Explain the provisions of the Companies Act 2013 relating to the appointment of the first auditor of a company, distinguishing a government company from other companies, and state how a casual vacancy in the office of auditor is filled. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: First auditor of a company other than a government company (s. 139(6)): appointed by the Board of Directors within thirty days from the date of registration of the company; on the Board's failure it shall inform the members, who shall within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting appoint the first auditor; in either case he holds office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting

First auditor of a government company or a company owned or controlled directly or indirectly by the Central Government, a State Government or Governments (s. 139(7)): appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India within sixty days from the date of registration; on his failure, by the Board within the next thirty days; on the Board's failure, by the members at an extraordinary general meeting within sixty days; he holds office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting

Subsequent auditor of such a company (s. 139(5)): appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India within one hundred and eighty days from the commencement of the financial year, to hold office till the conclusion of the annual general meeting

Casual vacancy (s. 139(8)): in a company other than one audited by a C&AG-appointed auditor, filled by the Board within thirty days, and where the vacancy results from the resignation of an auditor the appointment must also be approved by the company at a general meeting convened within three months of the Board's recommendation; in a company audited by a C&AG-appointed auditor, filled by the C&AG within thirty days and, on his failure, by the Board within the next thirty days; the auditor so appointed holds office till the conclusion of the next annual general meeting

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 139(2) to 139(4) · Rotation of auditors
questions.stem: State the provisions of the Companies Act 2013 relating to the rotation of auditors, including the classes of companies to which they apply, the maximum tenure, the cooling-off period and the anti-avoidance rules. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Application: no listed company, and no company belonging to such class or classes as may be prescribed, shall appoint or re-appoint an individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, or an audit firm as auditor for more than two terms of five consecutive years

Prescribed classes (rules-level, to be verified for the attempt): unlisted public companies having paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore or more; private companies having paid-up share capital of ₹50 crore or more; and companies having public borrowings from financial institutions, banks or public deposits of ₹50 crore or more

Cooling-off: an individual who has completed his term, and an audit firm which has completed two terms, shall not be eligible for re-appointment as auditor in the same company for five years from the completion of the term or terms
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 139(2), first and second provisos

skeleton.point: Anti-avoidance: as on the date of appointment no audit firm having a common partner or partners with an outgoing audit firm whose tenure expired in the immediately preceding financial year shall be appointed for five years; the same bar reaches a firm in the same network of audit firms, and a firm joined by the partner who was in charge of the outgoing audit and certified the financial statements; where joint auditors are appointed, rotation is so applied that all of them do not complete their terms in the same year
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 139(2), third proviso and Explanation

skeleton.point: Members may go further under s. 139(3) by resolving that the auditing partner and his team be rotated at specified intervals or that the audit be conducted by more than one auditor; the Central Government may prescribe the manner of rotation under s. 139(4); and every company existing at the commencement of the Act had three years to comply
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, ss. 139(3), 139(4) and the transition proviso to s. 139(2)

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 141 · Eligibility and disqualifications
questions.stem: State who is eligible for appointment as auditor of a company and enumerate the disqualifications under section 141(3) of the Companies Act 2013, giving the monetary limits where prescribed. What is the consequence of incurring a disqualification after appointment? (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Eligibility: only a chartered accountant may be appointed; a firm, including a limited liability partnership, may be appointed by its firm name where a majority of its partners practising in India are so qualified; and where a firm is appointed, only the partners who are chartered accountants are authorised to act and sign on its behalf

Status-based disqualifications: a body corporate, other than a limited liability partnership registered under the LLP Act 2008; an officer or employee of the company; and a person who is a partner of, or in the employment of, an officer or employee of the company

Interest-based disqualifications with the prescribed limits: a person, his relative or partner holding any security of or interest in the company, its subsidiary, its holding or associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company — a relative may hold securities of face value not exceeding ₹1,00,000, with corrective action within sixty days of a later acquisition; indebtedness to any of those companies in excess of ₹5,00,000; and a guarantee or security given in connection with a third person's indebtedness to any of them exceeding ₹1,00,000
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 141(3)(d), read with Rule 10

skeleton.point: Relationship and capacity disqualifications: a person or firm having, directly or indirectly, a business relationship of the prescribed nature, arm's-length commercial transactions in the ordinary course of business and permitted professional services being excluded; a person whose relative is a director or is in the employment of the company as a director or key managerial personnel; a person in full-time employment elsewhere, or a person or partner of a firm already holding appointment as auditor of more than twenty companies, excluding one-person, dormant and small companies and private companies with paid-up share capital below ₹100 crore; a person convicted of an offence involving fraud where ten years have not elapsed; and a person whose subsidiary, associate company or other entity is engaged in the services specified in s. 144 as on the date of appointment

Consequence of a later disqualification: where a person appointed as auditor incurs any of these disqualifications after his appointment, he shall vacate his office, and such vacation shall be deemed to be a casual vacancy in the office of the auditor, to be filled under s. 139(8)

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 140 · Removal, resignation and change on fraud
questions.stem: Explain the procedure for the removal of an auditor before the expiry of his term, the obligations of an auditor who resigns, and the circumstances in which the Tribunal may direct a company to change its auditor. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Removal before expiry of term (s. 140(1)): the auditor may be removed by a special resolution of the company after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government in the prescribed manner; the application is made in the prescribed form within thirty days of the Board's resolution and the general meeting for the special resolution is held within sixty days of receipt of the approval; the auditor concerned must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 140(1) read with Rule 7

skeleton.point: Resignation (s. 140(2) and (3)): an auditor who has resigned shall, within thirty days from the date of resignation, file a statement in the prescribed form with the company and the Registrar, and in the case of a government company or a company covered by s. 139(5) also with the Comptroller and Auditor-General, indicating the reasons and other relevant facts; failure attracts a penalty on the auditor, with a further penalty for each day of continuing failure subject to the prescribed maximum

Change directed on fraud (s. 140(5)): the Tribunal, suo motu or on an application by the Central Government or any person concerned, may direct the company to change its auditor if satisfied that he has directly or indirectly acted in a fraudulent manner or abetted or colluded in any fraud by or in relation to the company or its directors or officers; on the Central Government's application the Tribunal may within fifteen days order that he shall not function as auditor and the Central Government may appoint another auditor; the vacancy is deemed a casual vacancy; and an auditor against whom a final order is passed is not eligible for appointment as auditor of any company for five years and is also liable under s. 447
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 140(5) with Explanations and provisos

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 143 · Powers and duties of the auditor
questions.stem: Discuss the powers and duties of an auditor under section 143 of the Companies Act 2013, covering his right of access, the matters he must inquire into, and the principal contents of his report. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Right of access: every auditor has a right of access at all times to the books of account and vouchers of the company, whether kept at the registered office or at any other place, and is entitled to require from the officers such information and explanation as he considers necessary; the auditor of a holding company also has access to the records of all its subsidiaries and associate companies so far as it relates to the consolidation of financial statements
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 143(1) and its proviso

skeleton.point: Matters to be inquired into under s. 143(1): whether loans and advances made on the basis of security are properly secured and their terms not prejudicial; whether transactions represented merely by book entries are prejudicial; whether, for a company that is not an investment or banking company, shares, debentures and other securities have been sold below cost; whether loans and advances have been shown as deposits; whether personal expenses have been charged to revenue account; and whether cash was actually received where shares are stated to have been allotted for cash

The report: made to the members on the accounts examined and on every financial statement laid before the company, stating whether the accounts give a true and fair view of the state of affairs, of the profit or loss and of the cash flows, after taking into account the accounting and auditing standards; and stating the matters in s. 143(3) — information and explanations obtained, proper books of account and branch returns, the branch auditor's report and its treatment, agreement of the financial statements with the books, compliance with the accounting standards, adverse observations, directors' disqualification under s. 164(2), qualifications and adverse remarks, adequacy and operating effectiveness of internal financial controls, and the prescribed matters; reasons must be given wherever an answer is in the negative or qualified

Additional duties: compliance with the auditing standards under s. 143(9) and (10); branch audit and receipt of the branch auditor's report under s. 143(8); and in a government company, compliance with the C&AG's directions, the C&AG's right within sixty days of receiving the audit report to conduct a supplementary audit and to comment upon or supplement the report, and the power to order a test audit

questions.topic: Ch 10 · s. 143(12) to 143(15) · Reporting of fraud
questions.stem: State the auditor's duty to report fraud under section 143(12) of the Companies Act 2013, the time limits involved, and the consequences of a failure to report. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Trigger: where an auditor, in the course of the performance of his duties as auditor, has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving the prescribed amount is being or has been committed in the company by its officers or employees, he must report it; the prescribed amount is ₹1 crore or more for an individual fraud, in which case the report goes to the Central Government
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 143(12) read with Rule 13

skeleton.point: Procedure and time limits for a fraud of ₹1 crore or more: report to the Board or the audit committee immediately and not later than two days of knowledge, seeking their reply or observations within forty-five days; on receiving the reply, forward the report, the reply and his own comments to the Central Government within fifteen days of receipt; if no reply is received within the forty-five days, forward the report with a note to that effect within fifteen days of the expiry of that period, in the prescribed form

Fraud below the prescribed amount: report to the audit committee constituted under s. 177, or to the Board where there is no such committee, immediately and not later than two days of knowledge, specifying the nature of the fraud with a description, the approximate amount involved and the parties involved; and the company must disclose the details in the Board's report in the prescribed manner
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 143(12), first and second provisos

skeleton.point: Protection and penalty: no duty of the auditor is regarded as contravened by reason of reporting under s. 143(12) if done in good faith; the sub-section applies mutatis mutandis to the cost accountant conducting a cost audit under s. 148 and the company secretary in practice conducting a secretarial audit under s. 204; and a failure to comply attracts a penalty of ₹5,00,000 for a listed company and ₹1,00,000 for any other company

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Case: the appointment clocks of a newly registered company
questions.case: Chandravali Foods Limited, which is not a government company, is registered on 12 May 2026. Its Board of Directors takes no step to appoint an auditor within the period allowed by the Act and, on 20 June 2026, formally informs the members of its failure. The members later appoint a first auditor at an extraordinary general meeting. That auditor dies in office some months afterwards, and the Board meets to fill the resulting vacancy.

readLink.label: Read: The first auditor and casual vacancies →

questions.stem: The Board's failure is a failure to comply with which requirement?

options.text: To appoint the first auditor within sixty days from the date of registration
options.explanation: Sixty days is the C&AG's window for the first auditor of a GOVERNMENT company under s. 139(7). This company is not one.

options.text: To appoint the first auditor within thirty days from the date of registration
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(6) requires the Board of a company other than a government company to appoint the first auditor within thirty days from the date of registration — here, by 11 June 2026.

options.text: To appoint the first auditor within thirty days from the date of the first Board meeting
options.explanation: The clock runs from the date of REGISTRATION, not from any Board meeting. Delaying the first Board meeting cannot extend it.

options.text: To appoint the first auditor at the first annual general meeting
options.explanation: That is the s. 139(1) appointment, which the members make at the first annual general meeting. It is a different appointment from the first auditor under s. 139(6).

questions.stem: The last date by which the members must appoint the first auditor at an extraordinary general meeting is:

options.text: 20 July 2026
options.explanation: This counts thirty days, which is the Board's window, not the members'.

options.text: 19 August 2026
options.explanation: This counts sixty days. Sixty days is the members' window for a GOVERNMENT company under s. 139(7).

options.text: 18 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(6) gives the members ninety days from the Board's information; 20 June 2026 plus ninety days is 18 September 2026.

options.text: 20 September 2026
options.explanation: This reads the period as three calendar months. The section states ninety days, and days are counted as days.

questions.stem: The first auditor so appointed by the members holds office:

options.text: Till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Whether the first auditor is appointed by the Board or, on its failure, by the members, s. 139(6) ends his office at the conclusion of the first annual general meeting.

options.text: Till the conclusion of the sixth annual general meeting, the members having appointed him
options.explanation: The five-meeting term belongs to an appointment made under s. 139(1) at the first annual general meeting. The identity of the appointing body does not convert a first-auditor appointment into a s. 139(1) appointment.

options.text: For one year from the date of the extraordinary general meeting
options.explanation: The tenure ends at a meeting, not on an anniversary of the appointment.

options.text: Till the Central Government approves his removal under section 140(1)
options.explanation: That describes an early exit, not the natural tenure fixed by s. 139(6).

questions.stem: On the death of that auditor, the vacancy is to be filled:

options.text: By the members at an extraordinary general meeting within ninety days
options.explanation: The ninety-day members' route belongs to a first-auditor appointment after the Board's failure. A casual vacancy goes to the Board.

options.text: By the Board within thirty days, and the appointment must also be approved by the members within three months of the Board's recommendation
options.explanation: The members' approval is required only where the casual vacancy is a result of the RESIGNATION of an auditor. Death is not resignation.

options.text: By the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India within thirty days
options.explanation: That applies only to a company whose accounts are subject to audit by a C&AG-appointed auditor. This company is not one.

options.text: By the Board within thirty days, without any approval of the members, the auditor so appointed holding office till the conclusion of the next annual general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 139(8)(i) gives the Board thirty days; members' approval attaches only to a resignation-caused vacancy; and the tenure runs to the conclusion of the next annual general meeting.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Case: testing the section 141 disqualifications
questions.case: Tarangini Structures Limited proposes to appoint CA Meghna as its auditor at the annual general meeting to be held in September 2026. Three facts emerge on the eligibility check. First, her brother holds equity shares of the company of a face value of ₹1,20,000. Second, she is indebted to a wholly owned subsidiary of the company in the sum of ₹4,80,000 and is negotiating a further loan from that subsidiary. Third, she stays at a hotel operated by the company's associate company when she travels, paying the published tariff, and her firm also proposes to design and implement the company's new financial information system.

readLink.label: Read: Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications →

questions.stem: The brother's shareholding:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 141(3)(d)(i) and its provisos

options.text: Is irrelevant, because a brother is not a relative for the purposes of the Act
options.explanation: A brother falls within the statutory list of relatives, so the clause is engaged.

options.text: Is permitted, because a relative may hold securities of any face value so long as he is not a director
options.explanation: There is no such rule. The relief for a relative is capped by face value.

options.text: Exceeds the permitted face value of ₹1,00,000 and must be brought within the limit, corrective action being available within sixty days where the limit was crossed by an acquisition
options.explanation: Correct. The excess of ₹20,000 of face value takes the holding beyond the relief, and the sixty-day corrective window is the cure the proviso provides.

options.text: Disqualifies CA Meghna permanently, no corrective action being possible
options.explanation: The proviso expressly contemplates corrective action within sixty days. The disqualification is curable.

questions.stem: Her indebtedness of ₹4,80,000 to the company's wholly owned subsidiary:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 141(3)(d)(ii) read with Rule 10

options.text: Is within the prescribed limit of ₹5,00,000, but the limit applies to the company, its subsidiary, its holding and associate companies alike, so further borrowing may disqualify her
options.explanation: Correct. The clause reaches indebtedness to the company, its subsidiary, its holding company, its associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company, and the line is ₹5,00,000.

options.text: Is irrelevant, because the clause applies only to indebtedness to the company itself
options.explanation: The clause expressly extends to the subsidiary, holding and associate companies as well.

options.text: Already disqualifies her, the prescribed limit being ₹1,00,000
options.explanation: ₹1,00,000 is the limit for a relative's securities and for a guarantee given for a third person's debt. The indebtedness line is ₹5,00,000.

options.text: Disqualifies her only if she fails to repay it within sixty days of appointment
options.explanation: The sixty-day corrective window belongs to a relative's acquisition of securities under s. 141(3)(d)(i). Indebtedness has no such window; it is simply tested against the limit.

questions.stem: The maximum further amount CA Meghna may borrow from that subsidiary while remaining eligible for appointment is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 141(3)(d)(ii) read with Rule 10 (rules-level: ₹5,00,000)

options.explanation: This treats the limit as fresh headroom, ignoring the ₹4,80,000 already outstanding. The limit applies to total indebtedness.
₹1,00,000 is the relative's securities limit and the guarantee limit, not the indebtedness limit.

options.text: Nil — she is already disqualified
options.explanation: ₹4,80,000 does not exceed ₹5,00,000, so she is not yet disqualified and some headroom remains.
Correct. The permitted indebtedness is ₹5,00,000 and ₹4,80,000 is already outstanding, leaving headroom of ₹20,000; any borrowing beyond that takes her over the line.

questions.stem: On the hotel stays and the proposed financial information system work:

options.text: Both are fatal: the hotel stays are a business relationship and the system work is a prohibited service
options.explanation: The hotel stays are not fatal. Commercial transactions in the ordinary course of business at arm's length price, of the kind hotels, airlines and telecom companies enter into with their customers, are excluded from 'business relationship'.

options.text: The hotel stays at the published tariff are an excluded arm's-length commercial transaction, but designing and implementing a financial information system is a service prohibited by section 144
options.explanation: Correct. The business-relationship exclusion covers ordinary-course arm's-length transactions; the financial information system work is expressly in the s. 144 list, and under s. 141(3)(i) an entity engaged in such services as on the date of appointment also disqualifies.

options.text: Both are permissible, since section 144 services may be rendered with the approval of the Board
options.explanation: Board or audit committee approval permits OTHER services. It cannot authorise any of the services s. 144 prohibits.

options.text: Both are permissible, since neither the subsidiary nor the associate company is the company being audited
options.explanation: Both clauses expressly extend to the holding, subsidiary and associate companies, and s. 144 covers services rendered to the holding or subsidiary company as well.

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Case: fraud reporting and the cost audit chain
questions.case: On 4 May 2026 the auditor of Hemadri Polymers Limited, an unlisted company that has constituted an audit committee, forms the reason to believe that officers of the company have committed a fraud of ₹1.6 crore. He reports the matter to the audit committee within the time allowed, seeking their observations. No reply whatever is received from the audit committee or the Board. Separately, the company is covered by the cost-audit rules; its cost auditor notices the same transactions during the cost audit, and the company receives a copy of the cost audit report on 5 October 2026.

readLink.label: Read: Reporting of fraud →

questions.stem: Because the fraud involves ₹1.6 crore, the auditor is required to:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 143(12) read with Rule 13

options.text: Report first to the audit committee within two days of his knowledge seeking a reply within forty-five days, and thereafter report the matter to the Central Government
options.explanation: Correct. The amount being ₹1 crore or more, the ultimate recipient is the Central Government, but the first step is always the audit committee or Board within two days, with forty-five days for their reply.

options.text: Report only to the audit committee, the Board's report then disclosing the details
options.explanation: That is the route for a fraud BELOW the prescribed amount. Above it, the Central Government must be reached.

options.text: Report to the Central Government within two days of his knowledge, without approaching the audit committee
options.explanation: There is no direct-to-Government route. The internal report within two days is mandatory in every case.

options.text: Report to the Registrar of Companies and to the Tribunal
options.explanation: Neither is a recipient under s. 143(12). The Tribunal's role in relation to auditors arises under s. 140(5), on a different trigger.

questions.stem: The auditor reported to the audit committee on the last day permitted. No reply having been received, the last date by which he must forward his report to the Central Government is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 143(12) read with Rule 13

options.explanation: This adds only fifteen days to the internal report and ignores the forty-five-day reply period, which must expire before the Central Government clock starts where no reply comes.

options.text: 20 June 2026
options.explanation: This is the date the forty-five-day reply period expires. The auditor then gets a further fifteen days to forward the report.

options.text: 20 July 2026
options.explanation: This allows thirty days after the expiry of the reply period. The rule allows fifteen.

options.text: 5 July 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Knowledge on 4 May 2026, internal report by 6 May 2026 (two days), reply period expiring 20 June 2026 (forty-five days), and fifteen days more to forward the report — 5 July 2026.

questions.stem: As regards the cost auditor who noticed the same transactions:

options.text: He has no reporting duty, section 143(12) applying only to the auditor appointed under section 139
options.explanation: Section 143(14) applies s. 143(12) mutatis mutandis to the cost accountant conducting a cost audit and to the company secretary in practice conducting a secretarial audit.

options.text: The same obligation applies to him mutatis mutandis, independently of the statutory auditor, and a failure to comply exposes him to a penalty of ₹1,00,000, the company being unlisted
options.explanation: Correct. The duty is his own and is not discharged by the statutory auditor's report; s. 143(15) fixes the penalty at ₹5,00,000 for a listed company and ₹1,00,000 for any other.

options.text: He must report only to the Board, whatever the amount involved
options.explanation: The cost auditor's obligation mirrors the statutory auditor's in full, including the route to the Central Government above the prescribed amount.

options.text: His duty is discharged once the statutory auditor has reported the same fraud
options.explanation: The obligations are independent. Section 143(14) does not make one person's compliance a substitute for another's.

questions.stem: The last date by which the company must furnish the cost audit report to the Central Government is:

options.text: 20 October 2026
options.explanation: This counts fifteen days. Section 148(6) allows thirty.

options.text: 4 December 2026
options.explanation: This counts sixty days, a period that does not appear in s. 148.

options.text: 4 November 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days from the company's receipt of the report on 5 October 2026 expires on 4 November 2026, and the filing must carry full information and explanation on every reservation or qualification.

options.text: 3 April 2027
options.explanation: This counts 180 days, which is a rules-level period for the cost auditor to submit his report after the close of the financial year, not the company's filing window.
